title: NVIDIA releases Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open-weight speech model for 40 languages
subtitle: The MoE model handles transcription, translation, and speaker labeling for recordings up to an hour, with a 463,062-hour multilingual dataset released alongside it.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe as open weights on Hugging Face and ModelScope under the OpenMDW-1.1 license, with day-zero serving support in vLLM and NeMo Speech. The model covers 40 languages for transcription, translates among 31, labels up to eight speakers in audio up to an hour long, and answers questions about recordings in natural language. It does not handle live streams. Hosted access is already live on DeepInfra and OpenRouter.

The architecture is a mixture of experts with roughly 4B active parameters out of around 30B total — reports disagree on the exact total, with some citing 34B at 4.3B active. NVIDIA says the model placed first among open-weight entries on the Hugging Face Open ASR English leaderboard at 5.33% average WER, and Artificial Analysis lists it tied for first among open-weight models at 2.8% AA-WER. One independent evaluation snapshot gave 4.71% English WER, so the headline figure varies by test setup.

Alongside the model, NVIDIA released Granary v2, a 463,062-hour speech dataset covering 48 languages. For English speech recognition, the open-weight tier had been dominated by Whisper variants and a shrinking set of academic releases. A multilingual MoE with sub-5% WER, prompt-steered output (a plain-language request for a clean versus verbatim transcript), and a matching open dataset is a notable raising of the floor for anyone doing voice work on their own hardware.

A note for learners: speech models are one of the easiest places to run frontier capability on consumer hardware, and open-weight transcription is now good enough for most practical uses — meeting notes, podcast indexing, accessibility pipelines. If you are building anything that touches audio, download Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (or Whisper) and run it locally once before you reach for a hosted API. You will learn more about what the model actually does from one hour of local experimentation than from any benchmark table.
